Percentage Calculations

Enter a start and end to sum bin percentages.

Whole bins are selected when their midpoints lie between your start and end (inclusive). The result reports the actual covered bin boundaries.

Percentage histogramPercentage polygon (bin midpoints)
Point to a bar or polygon marker for its interval, count, and percentage.

The horizontal range is fixed across sample sizes. Each bin includes its lower boundary and excludes its upper boundary: [lower, upper). Percentage = bin count ÷ selected sample size × 100. The polygon joins midpoints and closes at zero one bin beyond each end.

Block 2 / Scaled percentage histogram and density

(Scaled) Percentage Polygon of a Single Broccoli Price

Point to a bin for its count, percentage, and density height.

Probability of a Broccoli Price in a Range

Probability is the area under the selected curve. Both mode shows the polygon and PDF estimates separately.

How the density and statistics are calculated

Bar height = 100 × bin count ÷ (selected sample size × bin width). The vertical axis is (Scaled) Percentage, and each bar’s area is the percentage in that bin. Total bar area is 100%.

The red polygon joins bin midpoints and closes at zero one bin width beyond the outer midpoints. It also encloses 100%. Its mean, variance, and standard deviation are calculated by exact integration of its straight segments. Statistic buttons show only the selected empirical value and do not display fitted-PDF moments. Changing bin width can change these estimates.

The dark-blue Probability Density Function (PDF) is a normal curve fitted to the selected raw prices using their arithmetic mean and sample standard deviation (n − 1 denominator). Its height is multiplied by 100 to match the histogram. PDF interval probabilities use a normal CDF approximation; polygon probabilities use exact trapezoid areas. Curve selection controls which estimates and shaded areas are shown.

Both blocks use the same cached prices: all 100,000 original observations remain at the start, and additional prices are seeded normal draws using the original mean and sample standard deviation. Their sample-size controls select prefixes of that shared cache. Changing bin width, curve mode, or probability bounds does not resample. Regenerating with a new seed rebuilds only the additional prices in both blocks; all original prices are preserved. Normal simulations can include negative values. Prices and bounds are in dollars, not thousands.
